findings: “Five came out at the top, a sixth of every dace in the book.” -> “Five came out at the top, a sixth of all the dace in the book.” (passage, paragraph 2; a fraction taken over the distributive quantifier 'every' with a count noun gives the literal reading 'a sixth of each dace' — 'all the dace' or 'one in every six dace' is what is meant)

“The remedy her argument points at is a second mouth on the right bank” -> “The remedy her argument points to is a second mouth on the right bank” (passage, paragraph 5; 'point at' is for physical targets, 'point to' for what evidence or an argument indicates)
justification: Read aloud end to end as a native, hunting for anything a native writer would not produce. The voice is consistent and strongly textured: named people (Elspeth Kelsingham, Adrian Kitson), a named place, dates, hard counts, dry wit ('Nobody says the pass does not work. What has taken fifteen years to become interesting is what it works for.'), varied sentence rhythm, no AI-essay boilerplate, no marketing cadence. The two quoted spans read as speech, with contractions ('The dace aren't beaten by the ladder', 'They don't find it', 'isn't a matter of opinion', 'It's on the record'). Two places made me stop: the partitive over 'every dace', and 'points at'. Specialist compressions I considered and cleared: 'let into the weir's left abutment', 'drown the weir out' (the correct hydrological term for a weir under high tailwater, not the sound sense), 'a long slack behind a shingle bar', 'came through the same water clear', 'antennas' (correct for radio aerials; 'antennae' would be the insect sense). Nothing lethal, so flag.

findings: “The remedy her argument points at” -> “The remedy her argument points to” (passage, paragraph 5; preposition choice, and the exact shape a Swedish 'peka på' calque takes)

justification: Systematic sweep of the known ELF failure classes over passage, prompts, options and rationales. Preposition calques: one hit ('points at'); 'turns on', 'speaks to', 'put down to', 'holds in the current' all correct. Countability: clean (no *informations/*researches/*evidences; 'grayling', 'dace', 'chub', 'trout' correctly zero-plural with plural agreement in 'The grayling make a different case'). False friends: none ('eventually', 'actual', 'rest' all used correctly — 'the rest in three others' is the remainder sense and is right). Articles: one definite first mention ('the box'); everything else correct, including bare 'Nobody', 'None of it'. Tense/aspect: clean, including the present-perfect/simple-past alternation between the fifteen-year record and the two tagged springs. Negative-polarity items: every one licensed — 'with little to tell it anything is there' (little), 'nothing here suggests the dace run is out of step with anything' (nothing), 'dace and grayling barely at all' (barely), 'Nothing here counts fish above the weir at all' (Nothing). Relative pronouns: no 'whom' anywhere; 'who' used only of Kelsingham and of readers, never of fish or objects. Zero relatives: all have gaps ('the year the mill ... finally stopped' is a time adjunct gap; 'A pass that one fish gets up easily' has an object gap). Pronoun reach: 'it came over the crest' takes 'the river' from the immediately preceding clause; 'too little flows from it' takes the nearest and intended 'the entrance'. Mixed comparisons: none — 'more dace than the trap has ever held' and 'More of them were tagged than of any other fish' both compare like with like. Comma splices: none; the 'the counts written into a hardbacked book' clause is an absolute, not a splice. Garden paths: 'drown the weir out' considered and cleared as the standing technical term. Arithmetic in the rationales checked against the passage and all of it reconciles (11+28=39 entrants, 7+5=12 out; 39+2=41 has no analogue here; 174/23/9/5 dace chain consistent). Two minor findings, nothing lethal.

findings: “B, kept, puts a past participle after worth, which gives the shape of worth said or worth doing badly and cannot govern the object open here.” -> “B, kept, puts a past participle after worth, and worth takes no past participle: worth kept open is no more English than worth said.” (gap (2) rationale; LETHAL — 'worth doing badly' is well-formed English and is a gerund, i.e. the very shape the same rationale endorses two sentences earlier, so it cannot illustrate the ungrammatical participle shape; and 'cannot govern the object open here' has no coherent subject)

“The sentence carries an explicit contrast, not because the village refused them but because, so what follows has to be a reason that is not refusal” -> “The sentence carries an explicit contrast — not because the village refused them but because — so what follows has to be a reason that is not refusal” (gap (4) rationale; the passage's words are cited inline with no quotation marks or dashes, so the sentence garden-paths as the writer's own causal claim and then dead-ends on 'but because,')

“a man carries a standard lamp out to a car on the grass, watched from the doorway by the woman who brought it” -> “... watched from the doorway by the woman who brought it in” (passage, final sentence; 'it' has to reach past 'a car on the grass' to find 'a standard lamp')
justification: Read aloud end to end as a native. The passage itself is very good: 'the hall smells of other people's wardrobes', 'the covering is low and even, the way a field is even after the pickers', 'the thing that was somebody's', and a closing image that lands. Named people, a named tenure ('fourteen years'), concrete objects, no boilerplate. The quoted speech reads as speech: 'Nobody's buying after four', 'They're doing us a favour, and I'd rather say so than pretend' — contractions in both, and a real speaker's shrug in the second. The read stops hard in the RATIONALE layer, twice. The gap (2) explanation is a grammar explanation that contradicts itself: it correctly states that worth takes a gerund, then offers 'worth doing badly' — a gerund, and perfectly good English — as an example of the bad participle shape. A learner who knows the Chesterton line will be actively misled by the item whose whole teaching point is worth + gerund. That is lethal. The gap (4) opening is unreadable on first pass because the cited words carry no marks. Kill.

findings: “of the brown already in the fibres she says “I can lighten. I don’t promise to take it out.”” -> “of the brown already in the fibres she says “The brown that’s in the fibres I can lighten. I don’t promise to take it out.”” (Q1 rationale, the paragraph on option D; LETHAL — the quoted span is not what the passage says, and as quoted 'I can lighten.' is a transitive verb standing with no object and no bracketed supply, which is not a sentence a native writer would set inside quotation marks)

“so C restates the passage’s mechanism in other words without lifting any run of them” -> “so C restates the passage’s mechanism in different words” (Q1 rationale, the paragraph on option C; 'them' has no correct antecedent — the nearest plural is 'other words', while the intended one is the passage's words — and 'lifting any run of them' is anti-plagiarism process vocabulary that has no business being shown to a student)

justification: Read aloud end to end as a native. The passage is the best-textured of the four for its length: a certificate in a tea towel, a date, three flakes of film, a hard brown band 'the width of the strip'. QUOTED VOICE — asked for specifically, judged specifically: it reads as a real person speaking, not written prose in quotation marks. The evidence is contractions in every sentence that can take one ('there's', 'What's', 'that's', 'the sheet's gone', 'won't', 'The glue's', 'it's', 'don't'); trade shorthand that only a working conservator uses ('so it's solvent'); and three object-frontings — 'A mend from last year I warm', 'One like this, heat won't shift', 'The brown that's in the fibres I can lighten' — which are contrastive topicalisations, a spoken pattern, and they cohere as one speaker's habit. 'Tape holds a tear for ten years and marks the sheet for a hundred' is composed, but it reads as the line she has said to a hundred clients, which is exactly right. Only note: three frontings inside about sixty words is dense; two would be safer. The read stops in the RATIONALE, where she is quoted saying 'I can lighten.' — a sentence she does not say and that no native writer would set in quotation marks with a full stop. That is lethal, and it is the kind of defect this lane keeps shipping on the rationale side. Kill.

findings: “Ralph Jarrett, a currier, stood against more loans than any other name.” -> “Ralph Jarrett, a currier, had more loans against his name than anybody else.” (passage; the appositive makes the subject a man, but only a name stands against loans in a ledger, and the comparison term is 'any other name', so a person is measured against names)

“The mark cont. was written against the entry” -> “The mark ‘cont.’ was written against the entry” (passage; an abbreviation being mentioned rather than used, set as plain running text, so the abbreviating full stop reads on first pass as the end of the sentence)
“B is the fine misread” -> “B is the fine misreading” (Q1 rationale; 'misread' as a noun is a register step down from the surrounding archival prose)
justification: Read aloud end to end as a native. The passage has real texture for a hundred-and-eighty-word history note: a saddler's shop, a currier, a market town twenty miles from navigable water, guineas, a slate rubbed clean every week, and the fine closing fact that the ledger named neither the servant nor the child. The rhythm varies and there is no boilerplate. Three places made me stop. 'The mark cont. was written' derails on the abbreviation's full stop. 'Ralph Jarrett, a currier, stood against more loans than any other name' yokes a man to a comparison among names — the metonymy is recoverable and rather good, but the apposition 'a currier' pulls the subject back to the person and the sentence will not hold both. 'the fine misread' reads as journalese in prose that is otherwise careful. Considered and cleared: 'a volume so claimed came in on the fourteenth day' (formal but correct), 'The second fortnight needed no asking' (idiomatic), 'the ledger named neither' (licensed). Nothing lethal, so flag.

findings: “Ralph Jarrett, a currier, stood against more loans than any other name.” -> “The name of Ralph Jarrett, a currier, stood against more loans than any other.” (passage; mixed comparison — the subject is presented as a person by its apposition and compared against 'any other name')
